newsitem.title: USA: Chrysler introduces revamped family sedans.
newsitem.headline: Chrysler introduces revamped family sedans.

text.p: Chrysler Corp on Wednesday introduced redesigned versions of its Chrysler Concorde and Dodge Intrepid family sedans, which it expects to sell at prices similar to the current models.
The strategy contrasts with the one pursued by Ford Motor Co, which in 1995 introduced a redesigned Taurus sedan with enhanced features and higher prices.

"Our concept is to keep them as affordable as possible and keep them in the same price range of today's models," Chrysler Vice Chairman Robert Lutz told reporters after the introduction of the models at the North American International Auto Show in Detroit.
The current price range for the models is between $20,000 and $26,000, Chrysler said.
Improved production processes will help keep prices down, even though the cars include new engine technology, Lutz said.
The cars, as well as two other models to be introduced later in the year, were the result of a 31-month development program, which cost Chrysler about $2.1 billion, the carmaker said.
Chrysler expects to sell 250,000 to 260,000 of the cars annually, with Intrepid accounting for about 50 percent of the sales and the other three models making up the rest.
The redesigned Intrepid and Concorde should be in showrooms in September, Lutz said.
On Tuesday, Chrysler introduced its Durango sport/utility vehicle by having it break through the floor of a mock-up of Chrysler's new corporate headquarters.
The following day, the family sedans were unveiled as a stylized thunderstorm, complete with rainfall, raged on stage of Cobo Hall. The theme of the presentation was "Lightning Strikes Twice."

The base models of both cars will be powered by an all- aluminum, 2.7-liter, 24-valve V-6 engine rated at 200 horsepower. The Concorde LXi and Intrepid ES will have 3.2-liter, 24-valve V-6 engines rated at 220 horsepower.
The cars have cross car beams at the front and rear suspension towers and instrument panel areas for a quieter though more rigid ride, Chrysler said.
The cars also include larger headlights, increased usable cargo room, platinum-tipped spark plugs and "coil-on-plug" ignition systems to eliminate tune-ups before 100,000 miles, Chrysler said.
Chrysler stressed that the two sedans are designed to appeal to different types of consumers, with Intrepid geared to slightly younger, less affluent buyers.
Chrysler will assemble the cars at its Bramalea, Ontario, plant. Lutz said it would add a third shift at the plant only if sales reached 310,000 to 330,000 vehicles.
Lutz admitted that Chrysler was introducing the cars at a time when the market for sedans was declining, with many buyers now opting for sport utility vehicles and other choices.
Still, Lutz said the decline in sedan sales was in part cyclical and could change with the next generation of car buyers.
"We know each generation rejects what its parents had," Lutz said.
